subject: Agriculture
title: Expiration Date Confusion
description: A 60-second lesson on Expiration Date Confusion.

hook.text: 'Best by,' 'sell by,' 'use by'—these labels confuse consumers so much that they throw out perfectly safe food.

buildup.text: Except for infant formula, expiration dates in the US are not federally regulated. They're manufacturer suggestions.

discovery.text: Most dates indicate peak quality, not safety. Yogurt is usually fine for weeks past its 'sell by' date.

twist.text: An estimated 20% of consumer food waste is driven by date label confusion—$29 billion of food thrown out in the US alone.

climax.text: Standardizing labels to 'BEST if used by' (quality) and 'USE by' (safety) could reduce waste significantly.

punchline.text: The label says 'best by.' Your brain reads 'poison after.' Billions of dollars wasted.

quiz.question: What percentage of consumer food waste is driven by date label confusion?

details.summary: Expiration date confusion causes billions of dollars in food waste annually because consumers misinterpret labels as safety warnings. This topic clarifies the difference between 'best before,' 'use by,' and 'sell by' dates and why reform is urgently needed.
details.whyItMatters: Up to 20% of household food waste in developed countries results from date label confusion. Most discarded food is perfectly safe to eat, making this one of the easiest food waste problems to solve.
takeaways: 'Best before' indicates quality, not safety—food is usually safe well after the date
Only 'use by' dates on high-risk foods indicate a genuine safety concern
Standardizing date labels could prevent millions of tons of unnecessary food waste

faq.question: What is the difference between 'best before' and 'use by' dates?
faq.answer: 'Best before' dates indicate when food may begin losing peak flavor or texture but is still safe to eat. 'Use by' dates appear on high-risk perishables like meat and dairy and indicate a genuine safety deadline.

faq.question: How much food waste do confusing date labels cause?
faq.answer: Studies estimate that date label confusion contributes to up to 20% of consumer-level food waste in developed countries. In the US alone, this translates to billions of dollars of safe, edible food thrown away unnecessarily each year.
